chapter: Split, hospital and decline of tap
title: The Hotcha Club declines under a new owner
summary: Asked about tap's decline, Green describes the old Hotcha Club being run down by a new owner, who left, so dancers lost a place to originate steps.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Chuck, I'd like you to talk a little bit about those days just prior to the time you went into the hospital and then during those days when you were in the hopsital, and what was happening basically, then, to the entertainment medium for tap dancing -- whether places were beginning to shut down -- what exactly was the -- set the story of tap dancing during those days.

This owner, this new owner -- he had bought the old Hacha Not-Shot Club, see, and turned it into a night club -- well, it was like a place of pleasure, see. Like, it had a gaming room, you know, and refreshments, and naturally it was very - how can you say -- I'll say an overwhelming place, you know, something like they have a place similar to it now, this Hawaii Kai. It's up there by the Winter Garden, Maha Key,

you see, on Broadway, across from the Urus and the Circle Theater. What is that -- I think -- theatrical -- it's right where the Capital Theater used to be, somewhere near the Ma Kellinger Theater there, you know. The Hot Shot Club used to resemble that place, the Hawaii Kai, you see. In fact, they got one of the performers that used to be in the original Hotcha Hot Shot Club -- he was in the show, you know, and he was an attraction, see, because they didn't what he was. They thought he was -- see, Tom Thumb was very popular then, that little one, it was -- he hadn't gotten married, see, and the Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey Circus, or something, and this guy -- what I was saying, he was an attraction to the Hotcha Hot Shot Club because people like to come there just to see him, you know. He's a little man, see, but you couldn't hardly know until you -- he was a man until you heard him saying, see. Well, he was only one part of it, but, to say about -- to stay on the story, this new owner, he -- I think he went away, or went somewhere, you know. He left the club and maintenance didn't keep it up, you see, because they moved out most of these valuable pieces and, you know, oh, there was -- it would be vintage today, you know. And they just let it run down, you know, because there was -- a lot of the personalities that wanted to be discovered used to come to this Hoofer's Club, see, and they started this working on a degree of originating tap dances, you see, and they wanted to get, like, on the

Monarchy, which they called a tour -- that was like touring the world, you see. Like you're going around the world -- they call that monarchy, see. And they wanted to make sure that everyone was enjoying their pleasures, you see, because society was more gigantic. I think society became anemic after that (unintelligible) these things -- Because I don't think that the Board of Health actually realized what was occurring, you know. By the time when they find it out, you know, they got the condemnation sign up there, you know, saying 'building condemned.' You understand? And some of them communities, though, they upheld the rights of some buildings. They said, "NO, no, that's not right. There's nothing wrong with this building," or something, you know. But there would be a leaky pipe or somethng, you never know -- escaping fumes, which if somebody comes in there with a cigar -- a lit cigar, you know, maybe one of the first floors would go out or something, you know.
